_comment_model: PRODUCTION TARGET. Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct: 30.5B total / 3.3B active MoE (Qwen3MoeForCausalLM, 48 layers, 128 experts, 8 per token), Apache 2.0, 262k context. Chosen over Qwen3-32B dense and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B because it is code-specialized with a purpose-built function-call format, and our harness is tool-driven and the RL stage is multi-turn tool use. The 3.3B active footprint is what makes it deployable on device: ~10x less compute per token than a 32B dense at comparable memory.
_comment_model_id:
WARM START from step 150 of this same run, not the raw Instruct base. Job 9229 trained 150 clean steps (loss 0.4243, epoch 0.0932, no NaN, no router collapse) before its node died, and those weights are intact: all 25 safetensors shards present, index and config present, and a full 456GB read of the checkpoint returned no unreadable bytes. Throwing that away would cost ~2.3h of 8xMI355X for nothing.

This is a warm start rather than a bit-exact resume, and the difference is the optimizer. The step-150 optimizer state exists but is a single consolidated 244GB FULL_STATE_DICT file, and loading it back is what killed every resume attempt with SIGBUS on all eight ranks across two nodes -- the bytes read fine, so it is host memory exhaustion materialising it, not corruption. So the AdamW moments and the LR/step counters are not recovered; warmup and the cosine schedule restart, and the first ~9% of the data is seen a second time. At step 150 of 1609, still inside the 241-step warmup, those moments are worth far less than the 150 steps of learning they would cost to reclaim.

model_revision below is ignored for a local directory (model_spec logs that it did) and is kept as the record of which base this lineage started from. To train from the raw base again, set model_id back to Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct.
_comment_model_revision: Hub commit b2cff646, resolved 2026-08-03 and verified against the downloaded snapshot: 16 shards, 18,867 tensors, all BF16, 30,532,122,624 parameters, 61,064,245,248 bytes. Without this key model_spec.resolve_model_identity refuses the load outright in production mode (UnpinnedModelError) and, in development, silently trains whatever the shared HF cache happens to hold -- on a cache several people write to, that is not a reproducible run.
_comment_no_midtrain: There is no Base variant of this model, nor of Qwen3-32B or Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Continued pretraining requires one (running it on an instruct model destroys instruction-following -- docs/EVAL_RESULTS.md), and the chat-vector residual requires a base/instruct PAIR. So the cpt recipe cannot reach production at all, and this trains instruct -> SFT -> RL, which is what Dr. Kernel and Kernel-Smith do anyway.
_comment_dataset_path_v5: v5: 206,000 rows / 490,174,073 tokens (207,782 built, minus 1,196 for the held-out eval split and 586 truncated targets) / 165,047 distinct targets over 11,793 tasks. 61.2% kernel and 38.8% replay by rows, but 14% replay by TOKENS -- which is the unit that matters, and the unit v4 was never measured in. The substantive change from v4 is shape coverage: v4 asked one question (improve this kernel) across all 38,460 of its kernel rows, and this asks six (optimize, repair, PyTorch-to-kernel, spec-to-kernel, dialect port, language), because the benchmark asks five and v4 had zero examples of three of them. Every kernel target passed a numerical gate on real gfx950; 2,806 reward-hacking targets that delegate to torch were removed, along with 81,550 cross-root duplicates and 53,923 redundant repair answers (9.24 per problem down to 1.95). Screened against a frozen index of the evaluation benchmark's own PyTorch sources and against the held-out probe set, neither of which v4 was. output_dir is _v5 so this run cannot overwrite v4 checkpoints. Read from the repository copy on $HOME rather than /shared_nfs: $HOME is shared NFS and visible from every compute node, /shared_nfs is mounted READ-ONLY on the login node so nothing can be staged there from here, and a 1.8GB dataset has none of the size problem that puts output_dir on /shared_nfs. One source of truth, and data/release/reassemble.sh reproduces exactly this file from a fresh checkout.
_comment_dataset_path: v4: 244,732 rows / ~606M estimated tokens (~830M real), built from 82,275 agentic episodes of which 40,590 reached correctness. The AMD-native side is 34,806 step-centric revisions plus 13,572 residual full trajectories -- disjoint by construction, since a full trajectory is emitted only when its episode produced no step row. Measured blend is 65.9% kernel / 21.5% chat / 12.3% coding by tokens, against a 70/17/13 target; chat running over is the safe direction, as the replay literature puts the forgetting-mitigation plateau at 25-30%. Chat replay is Tulu-3 (TuluTalk measures better but its full 808k mixture was never released) and coding replay is OpenCodeReasoning-2, chosen over OpenCodeInstruct because it carries R1 reasoning traces rather than bare instruction->code, and reasoning is the capability replay has to protect here.
_comment_eval_dataset_path: 899 rows, 0.44% of the corpus, held out by scripts/v5_split_eval.py and REMOVED from dataset_path (206,000 rows now, from 207,782); 32 of its math rows were themselves truncated and were replaced from the clean pool, so every group is at full size. Removed by content hash rather than line number, because the mixture upsamples scarce slices: a first pass that split on line number left 296 of the 900 held-out rows with a surviving duplicate in training, and hashing the message list removed all 1,196 copies. Verified: zero message-hash overlap between the two files. This exists because the run's top risk -- losing instruction-following while learning kernels -- was otherwise unobservable until the run ended, 1,609 optimizer steps and ~30h later, on the one failure mode already measured once at lr 1e-5. Rows are tagged by capability and loaded as one dataset per group, so the log carries eval_instruction_following_loss separately from eval_kernel_generate_loss; a pooled scalar cannot tell 'kernels improved, chat collapsed' from 'nothing moved', and those call for opposite decisions. instruction_following, chat and general_code are over-sampled relative to their share of the corpus because they are what the run risks losing rather than what it teaches. Cost is ~1% of wall clock at eval_steps 200 (9 evals of 899 rows at batch 1).
_comment_eval_on_start: true. Without it the first measurement is step 200, and because every later delta is computed against the FIRST observation, whatever the run cost in its first 200 steps would be silently absorbed into the baseline and become invisible to the retention alarm. A step-0 baseline is the untrained model, which is the only honest reference for 'did this run damage anything'. Stated explicitly here rather than left to the dataclass default, because a setting that only exists as a default is one nobody sees in a config diff.
_comment_batch: global batch 128 = 2 x 8 x 8 ranks. per_device was 1 on the theory that MoE activation memory tracks the 8 routed experts rather than the 3.3B active figure; the smoke run measured 120GB of 288GB per GPU, so that was over-cautious by more than half. Raising it to 2 halves the micro-batches per optimizer step (16 -> 8), which is where the 119.87 s/step went: the step is dominated by per-micro-batch overhead, not arithmetic. Left at 2 rather than 4 because the smoke measured a 200-row slice at seq 17408, and the full mixture's p90 sequences are longer.
_comment_max_seq_length: 17408 matches the mixture, which is filtered to it. The model supports 262144, but raising this would not add data and would cost activation memory.
_comment_epochs_and_lr: 5e-6, and the honest justification is batch scaling, NOT the collapse this file used to cite. CORRECTION: the '1e-5 collapsed instruction-following' claim repeated here and in sft_14b_*.json describes docs/EVAL_RESULTS.md, which is a 14B DENSE model under CONTINUED PRETRAINING on raw text, cancelled at epoch 1.29, whose failure was output-surface destruction (29 of 33 responses not valid Python; correct kernels 23/34 -> 0/34). That is a different model, a different objective, and a different loss surface -- CPT puts gradient on every token while this puts it on the 38.6% inside assistant turns. 1e-5 has never been tested for chat-formatted SFT on this model, so nothing here bounds it, and the earlier corpus also still contained degenerate targets, reward hacks and the step-centric loss trap, any of which damages a model on its own and faster at higher LR. The number survives anyway on independent grounds. Nemotron-Cascade-2 trains this same 30B/3B-active architecture at 5e-5, but at 64 x 256k = 16.4M tokens per step against our 128 x ~2,379 = 305k, i.e. a 53.5x larger batch: sqrt-scaled that is 6.8e-6 and linearly scaled 9.4e-7, so the external band is 9.4e-7 to 6.8e-6 and 5e-6 sits inside it at 0.73x the sqrt-scaled value. The remaining discount is warranted because their 5e-5 starts from a BASE model while this starts from Instruct, and because replay is 12.0% of tokens (it was 13.9% before 9.3M tokens of truncated math chain-of-thought were removed as unfit targets; this is the single largest remaining deviation from best practice in this config, and the mitigation is the held-out eval rather than a guess -- if retained losses climb, add replay) against the 25-30% forgetting plateau -- forgetting scales with LR x steps x (1 - replay_fraction), so being under-replayed makes LR the compensating lever. The 10x gap in the headline numbers is a batch-size illusion, not a recipe disagreement. ONE epoch, for operational reasons: 206,000 rows / global batch 128 is 1,609 steps (earlier notes said 478 and then 1,867; 478 was wrong and 1,867 was correct only while repair_loss_weight=2.0 duplicated rows to 239,008, which it no longer does). A second epoch crosses the 23h walltime. This is a cold start for RL, which is where capability actually comes from, so a second epoch is a cheap continuation later -- and eval_dataset_path now makes 'is it undertrained' a measurement rather than a guess: if kernel loss is still falling at step 1400 of 1,609 with retained capabilities flat, continue; if retained losses climb while kernel falls, the alarm fires and the answer is more replay, not less LR.
_comment_lr_floor: cosine_with_min_lr holding 10% of peak, not a plain cosine to zero. Two reasons. The tail of a 1,609-step run at an LR approaching zero contributes almost nothing, and more importantly this checkpoint is a cold start for RL rather than a finished model -- a schedule that lands on exactly zero produces weights that are awkward to continue from. min_lr_rate 0.1 matches Nemotron-Cascade-2, which is the closest published recipe on this exact architecture (30B total / 3B active MoE).
_comment_warmup_ratio: 0.15, not the 0.03 dense default, which is 241 absolute steps of 1,609. Absolute steps are the unit that matters and 242 lands close to Nemotron-Cascade-2's 200 on this same architecture; an earlier note here claimed 'published MoE fine-tuning guidance is consistently 0.10-0.15', which could not be substantiated from any primary source -- the primary sources report absolute warmup steps, not ratios, so treat the ratio as a way of arriving at ~242 rather than as the recipe. The mechanism is the ROUTER: a small linear layer whose top-8-of-128 selection decides which experts see gradient at all, so a large early step can concentrate it on a subset before the loss has said anything useful. CORRECTION to the original reasoning: it claimed the experts the router stops selecting 'receive no gradient to recover with'. That is wrong -- the gate softmax is over all 128 logits, so every expert's ROUTER LOGIT keeps receiving gradient through the normalisation even when unselected. What actually freezes is the unselected experts' FFN weights, and for a 1,609-step narrow-domain SFT leaving most expert weights at their pretrained values is arguably desirable rather than a failure. The warmup is still justified, just by router stability rather than by expert starvation. Routing is now instrumented (per-layer load entropy, max-expert share, dead-expert count, reset per optimizer step), so this stops being an article of faith.
_comment_max_grad_norm: 0.5, tighter than the 1.0 HF default this config was silently inheriting by not naming it. Same reason as the warmup: routing instability. A gradient spike that would merely be noise in a dense model can permanently re-route tokens in an MoE, and the standard MoE recommendation is half the dense clip. Cheap insurance -- on a healthy run the clip rarely binds, and v3's observed grad_norm sat at 0.2-0.6 with only the warmup spike at 6.05 exceeding it.
_comment_packing: false, and it must stay false while the attention backend is SDPA. Packing concatenates several examples into one sequence and relies on the attention mask to keep them apart; on SDPA that isolation is not reliable and documents cross-contaminate, which degrades quality silently rather than erroring. kore/policy/sft.py already refuses to enable it outside flash_attention_2, and flash_attn is not installed in this venv. The throughput case for packing is real but was argued from the wrong number: the mixture mean is 2,394 tokens, and because group_by_length is on and the collator pads to the longest row IN BATCH, measured padding is 0.5% -- not the ~86% that comparing the mean to the 17,408 limit implies. What packing would actually buy is tokens per micro-batch: the MoE block is a Python loop over hit experts whose cost is independent of sequence length, so ~7 documents per packed sequence amortises the same ~6,144 loop iterations over 7x the useful work. That needs flash-attention, and it is its own experiment, not a change to make in a launch window.
_comment_repair_loss_weight: 1.0, i.e. OFF, down from 2.0. The weight duplicates whole rows, and repair rows average 4,067 tokens against a 2,418 corpus mean, so a 2x row duplication was a 1.6x token-mass amplification of the largest slice: repair went from 25.3% to 40.3% of trained tokens while replay+general fell from 13.9% to 11.1%. Instruction-following collapse is this run's stated top risk and was measured once already at lr 1e-5, and forgetting scales with LR x steps x (1 - replay_fraction) -- so diluting replay to 11% was pushing on the same failure from the other side. Repair is a quarter of the corpus without any help.
_comment_adam_beta2: 0.98, not the 0.999 default. Shortens the second-moment window, which is the standard mitigation for the loss spikes MoE routing instability produces -- the same failure max_grad_norm 0.5 exists to catch. Nemotron-Cascade-2 uses 0.98 on this architecture. Unmeasured here, low risk.
_comment_report_to: tensorboard, writing locally to logging_dir. No network needed. A 1,609-step run with 37 checkpoints and a known collapse risk should not leave loss-curve questions to log archaeology, and the routing-entropy series the new hooks emit is only readable as a curve.
_comment_save: save_total_limit is 2. Adam keeps ~16 bytes/param (fp32 weights, grads, m, v), so a 30.5B checkpoint is ~488GB against the 14B's 221GB, and because the Trainer writes the new checkpoint BEFORE rotating the old one out, limit=2 transiently holds three for a peak near ~1.46TB. /shared_nfs has 42T free, so that is 3.5% of it. This was 1 on a stale premise (~1090GB free, where the ~976GB two-checkpoint peak barely fit); at 42T that constraint no longer exists, and limit=1 was the riskier setting on a run that expects preemption, because the rotation window is precisely when a kill leaves nothing resumable. The volume is SHARED, so the space is not guaranteed to stay free: run 33992 died at step 400 with 'Disk quota exceeded' after another user consumed the margin underneath a write, which is why save_only_model remains available as the ~61GB fallback.
_comment_save_steps: 25, lowered from 50 now that a save is sharded rather than a 456GB rank-0 gather. Two things changed the arithmetic. First, cost: FULL_STATE_DICT wrote 456GB through one rank in a measured 7.5 minutes (checkpoint-100 19:24:41-19:32:26, checkpoint-150 20:18:23-20:25:38), which is what made 50 the right spacing; SHARDED_STATE_DICT writes ~366GB as eight per-rank slices in parallel and drops the redundant 122GB consolidated safetensors copy, so a save no longer dominates. Second, risk: this cluster is currently losing the node under us every 10-30 minutes (jobs 10849/...301, 10886/...297, 10942/...296, 10987/...331, 11155/...291 all NODE_FAIL), and at 50 the first checkpoint is ~57 minutes out -- longer than the node survives -- so the run would keep restarting from step 0 forever and never bank any progress. At 25 the first checkpoint lands around 34 minutes and each failure costs at most ~22 minutes. Raise this back toward 50 once nodes stop dying mid-run.
_comment_save_only_model: false, deliberately, after establishing what the failure actually was. Run 33992 died at step 400 with 'Disk quota exceeded (os error 122)' having written 4 of 25 shards, and the obvious reading -- a per-user quota we had exhausted -- is wrong. Both volumes are NFSv3 with no quota tooling present, and NFSv3 servers report a FULL VOLUME as EDQUOT. /shared_nfs is shared and its free space swung from ~0 to 5T to 17T within hours of the failure, so the write hit a moment when other users had consumed everything. There is no cap on what we may use. Dropping optimizer state would shrink the write 8x but costs resumability, and buying a smaller failure window by making every failure unrecoverable is the wrong trade when the space is genuinely there: 17T is ~35x one checkpoint and ~17x the 976GB rotation peak. Keep full checkpoints so a killed run resumes instead of restarting.
_comment_fsdp: fsdp_transformer_layer_cls is set explicitly for MoE. With auto_wrap and a null class the policy can wrap at the wrong granularity for Qwen3MoeDecoderLayer, which either shards the 128 experts badly or leaves whole layers unsharded and OOMs.
_comment_dataloader_num_workers: 2, lowered from 4 together with the sbatch's --cpus-per-task 128 -> 32. The CPU cut is what let the job be scheduled at all: 42 jobs submitted after ours started while a 128-CPU request went unplaced, because jobs asking 1-32 CPUs are placed continuously and 128 excludes most of a cluster whose CPU pool is genuinely contended. With 32 CPUs, 8 rank processes plus 2 workers each is 24 processes -- comfortable -- where 4 each would have been 40 and oversubscribed. Per-step host work is loading two pre-tokenised rows per rank and padding them, so 2 workers is not a throughput constraint; the GPU-side MoE expert loop dominates step time.
_comment_dataset_num_proc: 16, matching the smaller CPU allocation. This only affects TRL's one-time dataset map (~35s at 32 procs, a few minutes at 16) and is paid once against a run measured in tens of hours.
_comment_output_dir: On /shared_nfs, not /home. A 30B checkpoint is ~488GB and the Trainer writes the new one before deleting the old, so save_total_limit=2 peaks near ~1.46TB during rotation. /home is a 10TB volume shared with the whole cluster and sat at 310GB free when this was set -- our own footprint is only ~154GB, so the pressure is other users and not something we can reclaim. /shared_nfs has 42T free as measured before this launch, which is why save_total_limit could go back to 2; the figure has been stale three times in this file, so re-measure it rather than trusting this sentence. Training on /home would have died mid-rotation hours in, having burned the allocation.
_comment_dataset_path_v3: v3: 69,851 rows / ~255M tokens. Adds 4,279 AMD-NATIVE step-centric rows -- single revisions distilled from 11,227 multi-turn trajectories generated on MI355X through KoreEnv against AITER/hipBLASLt production baselines, keeping only correctness-preserving high-gain ones (1,499 fixes, 2,812 speedups). That 22.6% survival rate is the Kernel-Smith filter working as intended: training a local improver means discarding the revisions that were not improvements. Plus 4,493 recovered rows and the 61,079-row v2 base. All three sources passed one decontamination gate with ZERO held-out hits.
